However, Popper's own formal attempt to define verisimilitude logically failed because it was shown (by Tichý and Miller in 1974) that under standard logical definitions, a false theory with more content cannot be compared as 'closer to the truth' than another false theory unless one entails the other. Since most scientific theories are strictly false (as Popper admitted), the concept of verisimilitude collapses into incoherence without probabilistic assumptions about the distribution of truth-values or content, which Popper explicitly rejected. Therefore, the preference smuggles in induction because the only coherent way to interpret 'better corroboration' as a guide to future action is to assume the future will resemble the past (induction), rendering the 'non-inductive' claim untenable.", "outcome": "raised and not answered; the target's status did not move"}
